blocks.prompt: 11. If \(z = x + iy\) and \(\arg(z - 2 - 3i) - \arg(z + 2 + 3i) = 2\pi\), show that \(2y = 3x\).
blocks.explanation:
A locus question with a difference of two arguments.
Plan: the difference of arguments is the argument of the quotient. Then decide honestly what an argument of \(2\pi\) means, write the quotient in a + ib form and set its imaginary part to 0.
steps:
Given: \(z = x + iy\), \(\arg(z - 2 - 3i) - \arg(z + 2 + 3i) = 2\pi\).
To prove: \(2y = 3x\).
Method: \(\arg z_1 - \arg z_2 = \arg\frac{z_1}{z_2}\) (from the quotient rule of polar form).

Step 1: Combine the two arguments
\[\arg\left(\dfrac{z - 2 - 3i}{z + 2 + 3i}\right) = 2\pi\]
Why: dividing in polar form subtracts the arguments.

Step 2: What an argument of 2π means
\(2\pi\) is a full turn, the same direction as \(0\): along the positive real axis. So the quotient must be a positive real number: imaginary part \(= 0\) and real part \(> 0\).
Why: an argument is fixed only up to whole turns, so \(2\pi\) and \(0\) give the same direction. (If both arguments were principal values in \((-\pi, \pi]\), their difference would lie strictly between \(-2\pi\) and \(2\pi\) and could never equal \(2\pi\); the question only makes sense with this "full turn" reading.)

Step 3: Write top and bottom in a + ib form
\[z - 2 - 3i = (x - 2) + (y - 3)i\]
\[z + 2 + 3i = (x + 2) + (y + 3)i\]
Why: put \(z = x + iy\) and group real and imaginary parts.

Step 4: Multiply the top by the conjugate of the bottom
Conjugate of the bottom: \((x + 2) - (y + 3)i\). For \((a + bi)(c - di)\) the imaginary part is \(bc - ad\):
\[\text{Im} = (y - 3)(x + 2) - (x - 2)(y + 3)\]
\[= (xy + 2y - 3x - 6)\]
\[\quad - (xy + 3x - 2y - 6)\]
\[= 4y - 6x\]
Why: the new bottom \((x+2)^{2} + (y+3)^{2}\) is positive, so the quotient is real exactly when this imaginary part is 0.

Step 5: Set the imaginary part to zero
\[4y - 6x = 0\]
\[4y = 6x\]
\[2y = 3x\]
Why: a real number has no imaginary part; then divide both sides by 2.

Step 6: An honest check of the "positive" condition
The real part of the new top is
\[(x - 2)(x + 2) + (y - 3)(y + 3)\]
\[= x^{2} + y^{2} - 13\]
It must be positive, so \(x^{2} + y^{2} > 13\).
Why: the points \(2 + 3i\) and \(-2 - 3i\) lie on the line \(2y = 3x\) at distance \(\sqrt{13}\) from O. Between them (e.g. \(z = 0\)) the quotient is \(\frac{-2 - 3i}{2 + 3i} = -1\), a negative number: there the two arguments differ by \(\pi\), not \(2\pi\). Outside them (e.g. \(z = 4 + 6i\)) the quotient is \(\frac{2 + 3i}{6 + 9i} = \frac{1}{3} > 0\). ✓
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: \(2y = 3x\). (Every point satisfying the condition lies on this line; precisely, only on the parts of it outside the segment joining \(-2 - 3i\) and \(2 + 3i\).)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Does the printed claim hold? Yes, in this sense: reading an argument difference of \(2\pi\) as "a full turn, the same direction as 0", every \(z\) that satisfies the condition lies on the line \(2y = 3x\), which is what the question asks us to show. But the converse is not true: not every point of the line works. Points between \(-2 - 3i\) and \(2 + 3i\) give an argument difference of \(\pm\pi\), and the two end points themselves make one argument undefined. If the book's principal arguments in \((-\pi, \pi]\) are used strictly, a difference of exactly \(2\pi\) is impossible and no \(z\) satisfies the equation at all.
